docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Welcome to my Documentation Hub. This is where all my documentation regarding my current Raspberry Pi and Proxmox server Projects are hosted.

This allows me to share the work I have done, and all the steps and configuration. This is hosted via GitHub Pages, with the site pages created using MKDocs (with Material).

Any configuration files that are shareable, will be held on my GitHub repo, named Pi-Homelab. You can get to this using the link found at the top-right corner of the site.

To get started, click on any of the left-side tabs.

docs.title: 1. Initial Connection Setup
docs.text: For displaying and presenting my configs, documentation, and GitHub Pages, setting up GitHub on the Raspberry Pi is key. This is how I am currently hosting my documentation, as well as my configuration on the repo.

docs.title: Deployment of the GitHub Package
docs.text:
Ensure first that github is installed on the device:

sudo apt install git -y

We can then run through the following commands, to set our global username and email address. Enter your personal username and email address in place of "user" and "user@mail.com":

git config --global user.name "user"
git config --global user.email "user@mail.com"

To view what has been set:

git config --list

docs.title: SSH Key
docs.text:
To avoid entering your username and password every time you interact with remote repositories, we can setup an SSH key, so that this automatically authenticates with the device (Raspberry Pi).

To do this, we can generate the key using the following command:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "user@mail.com"
  • When prompted, you can press enter for the default path
  • It will also prompt you for a passphrase. Press enter to skip if not needed

SSH Key under /home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Pass Phrase is: Enter Pass Phrase

We can then copy the SSH key to our clipboard, so we can add it to github. We can use a tool called xclip to do this:

sudo apt install xclip -y
xclip -sel clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

We can then paste this into the new SSH Key entry that we will add on GitHub:

  1. Login to Github
  2. Click on your Profile Picture and select Settings
  3. Click on the SSH and GPG keys tab
  4. Click New SSH key
  5. Enter the name of the key, which will be Raspberry Pi 4 Git Key, and the copied SSH key
  6. Press Add SSH Key

We can test the connection via the following command:

ssh -T git@github.com

It will appear with a warning to say it can't be established, but press yes to trust the key. It will then ask for your pass phrase, and confirm connection.

docs.title: 1. Installation & Setup
docs.text: Vaultwarden is used to locally host your own Bitwarden Password Manager. This will be installed via a Docker Compose installation.

docs.title: Docker Compose Creation
docs.text:
Firstly, we can create out .yaml compose file under directory /home/home/PiProject-homelab/vaultwarden, as this can be a file we're happy to share to GitHub. The following is to be entered on the file:

sudo nano vaultwarden-compose.yaml

services:
  vaultwarden:
    image: vaultwarden/server:latest
    container_name: vaultwarden
    restart: unless-stopped
    dns:
      - 172.21.0.3 # To ensure Vaultwarden uses Unbound (Docker IP)
      - 192.168.x.x # Fallback to Pi IP as DNS
    environment:
      DOMAIN: ${DOMAIN}  # enter your domain
      SIGNUPS_ALLOWED: "false"                  # disable after creating your first account
      ADMIN_TOKEN: ${ARGON2_HASH}
    volumes:
      - /home/user/PiProject-homelab-data/vaultwarden:/data
    ports:
      - "${PORT}:80/tcp"

docs.title: Admin Token
docs.text:
For 'ADMIN_TOKEN', as we're hosting this file on Github, I have created a .env file to keep this on, with ${ARGON2_HASH} being called from it.

Under the same directory, I have ran sudo nano .env, and added the following inside:

ARGON2_HASH='INSERT_HASH_HERE'
DOMAIN=vault.user.local

docs.title: Generating encrypted ARGON2 Hash
docs.text:
To obtain and securely generate the ARGON2 hash code, we can generate a PHC code using Bitwarden defaults. There are a few methods of doing this, but the simplest is creating a temporary docker container:

docker run --rm -it vaultwarden/server:latest /vaultwarden hash

This will prompt for a password upon running the command; Enter a secure password (this will be your admin password). The output will then generate something similar to this:

$argon2id$v=14$n=233421,t=3,p=8$kK31413FFEsfCxSDdddwCF9LYXqrP312WERWgh2asdaff3E8ozeV+fsf324fgg5aJrRax4324fDVVDns8M

Paste what is generated into the env file, but making sure the single quotes are used at the start and end of the token.

Once the compose file is setup and ready, and setting the port number to be used, we can run the installation:

sudo docker compose -f vaultwarden-compose.yaml up -d

docs.title: HTTPS Setup
docs.text:
As Vaultwarden requires HTTPS to function, and allow you onto the vault, we have to make sure this is setup on our reverse proxy, Nginx.

Please refer to [Vaultwarden Server Block], and HTTPS steps breakdown via [4. HTTPS Configuration].

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Once HTTPS is setup, we can proceed on creating our login. On the browser, enter address vault.user.local.

On loading up the webpage, you will be presented with the Vaultwarden login interface. As this is a selfhosted Bitwarden vault, you won't be able to use an existing Bitwarden account. Therefore, we will need to create a new login.

Click Create Account, and setup your login.

![[Pasted image 20260818212702.png|406]]

docs.title: Exporting and Importing Passwords
docs.text: Once in, we can import our passwords. If you have password stored on a normal Bitwarden account, you can export these via the portal to a .json file.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Tools > Export
  2. Select file format .json
  3. Press Export, and select the area on your machine you'd like to store the file on

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Tools > Import
  2. Under Destination, select My vault, and leave the folder blank
  3. Under Data, select file format Bitwarden (json), and click Choose file
  4. Select the .json file on your machine, and press Import

When imported, all passwords should successfully transfer onto the account.

docs.title: Updating Vaulwarden
docs.text:
As for all docker containers, please ensure that the containers are updated with the latest image!!

We can tell if it is out-of-date, due to the browser extensions, mobile app, and desktop app of Bitwarden are not successfully pulling the passwords, and can also be checked via https://vault.user.local/admin/diagnostics.

Simply run the command below to pull the latest image, and then stop the container, delete the container, and reinstall it again from the compose.yaml file:

docker pull vaultwarden/server:latest

docs.title: 1. Installation for Pihole
docs.text: To install Pihole, we can use Docker Compose. This will allow us to use a .yaml file, which also contains the Unbound DNS container, that can work alongside Pihole.

docs.title: File Structures
docs.text:
As for the location of the file, we will store this via /home/user/raspberrypi-homelab/pihole-unbound, as this is the publicly available GitHub repository, and a file we would like to share.

We specifically want the Pihole and Unbound data files to be stored under PiProject-homelab-data. This can be specified in the piholeunbound-compose.yaml file itself.

We can then copy any files we want to share on our GitHub page to /home/user/PiProject-homelab. These files were created under the GitHub branch of my guides, from [2. Project Repository Setup], and an explanation of both folders, and their purposes, can be found here: [3. Shared Repository Files].

docs.title: Docker Compose File
docs.text:
The following config is to be entered within the .yaml file:

services:
  pihole:
    container_name: pihole # Can be named anything
    image: pihole/pihole:latest
    ports:
      - "53:53/tcp" # The DNS port
      - "53:53/udp"
      - "591:80/tcp" # 80 is the HTTP port it will listen on, whilst 591 will be the port it directs the traffic too. This is for the Web Interface, and 591 is the port I chose for this.
      - "${PORT}:443/tcp" # The HTTPS ports
    environment:
      TZ: "YOUR_TIMEZONE"
      FTLCONF_webserver_api_password: ${PIHOLE_PASSWORD}  # This points to the .env file, which contains the password it pulls. This is so this .yaml file can be safely shared on GitHub, without exposing my password.
      DNSMASQ_LISTENING: "all"
      PIHOLE_DNS_1: "unbound#53"  # Point to unbound container
    volumes:
      - /home/user/PiProject-homelab-data/pihole:/etc/pihole # Pihole files stored in host raspberrypi-homelab-data, and container will mirror this in /etc/
      - /home/user/PiProject-homelab-data/dnsmasq.d:/etc/dnsmasq.d
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      dns_network:
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
      - NET_RAW
      - CAP_SYS_NICE
      - CAP_SYS_TIME
    security_opt:
      - seccomp:unconfined
    depends_on:
      - unbound
  unbound:
    container_name: unbound2026050
    image: klutchell/unbound:latest
    volumes:
      - /home/user/PiProject-homelab-data/unbound:/etc/unbound/custom.conf.d # Unbound files stored in host raspberrypi-homelab-data, and container will mirror this in /etc/
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      dns_network:
networks:
  dns_network:
    driver: bridge
  • Check comments with # for short descriptions

docs.title: .env File
docs.text:
Note: For the password in this configuration, it is finding and using a created variable. We can just set a plain text password, but we can use this instead if sharing this config on GitHub, so it is hidden. To do this, create a new file in the same location named .env, and enter the following in it's file:

PIHOLE_PASSWORD=INSERT_HERE

INSERT_HERE can be replaced with the chosen password. .env is used, as GitHub is setup to ignore and not pull any .env files, as specified in it's .gitignore file, under /home/fooney/raspberrypi-homelab.

docs.title: Deploying the compose file
docs.text:
Once this file(s) have been created, and config lines used above, we can then initiate it's installation via the following command:

sudo docker compose -f piholeunbound-compose.yaml up -d

Wait for the installation to finalise. Once finished, we can check that both the Unbound and Pihole containers are running via sudo docker ps.

docs.title: Updating Pihole/Unbound
docs.text:
As for all docker containers, please ensure that the containers are updated with the latest image!!

We can check if this is out of date, via the portal itself at the bottom of the page. This will note as Update Available.

Run the following command to pull the latest image, and then stopping and deleting the current containers, before installing again via the compose file:

docker pull pihole/pihole:latest
docker pull klutchell/unbound:latest

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text: Nginx is a reverse proxy, which can be used to redirect IP Addresses with different ports, to different local domains setup in Pihole.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
In this case, we have our Raspberry Pi IP 192.168.0.x. As we have multiple services running, with different web interfaces, we won't be able to setup multiple local domains normally, as they all use the same IP Address. All the services running on docker containers however use different ports. This is where Nginx comes in.

The following can be setup: Pihole for example can use port 7000, whereas Vaultwarden uses port 6000. We can get Nginx to assign local domain pihole.user.local to 192.168.0.x:7000, and local domain vault.user.local to 192.168.1.x:6000.

This will use HTTP, but we can also configure it to use HTTPS, using self-signed certificates. These will all be setup in a configuration file, which I will guide through in this Nginx section.

docs.title: Package Install Command
docs.text:
First, we will need to install Nginx on our Pi. To do this, we can run the following command:

sudo apt install nginx -y

In this case, I have decided to not install nginx in a docker container, so that it is easier for setting up, and easier to communicate with the services.

docs.title: 1. Portainer Agent Installation
docs.text:
The Portainer Agent will allow us to have our Raspberry Pi Docker Containers manageable via the Portainer web portal, hosted on the Debian VM on our Proxmox Server.

To set up our agent, we first need to make sure the Portainer Server is setup, which you can refer to the guide [Proxmox/Debian VM (Docker Server)/Portainer/1. Installation]. Once this is confirmed all up and running on it's host server, we can begin.

docs.title: Setup via Portainer Server
docs.text:
Firstly, login to the Portainer Web Portal via your chosen IP/local domain.

Once in, navigate through to Environment-related > Environments > Click Add Environment. We can then walk through the following steps:

  1. Select Docker Standalone, and press Start Wizard
  2. Ensure Edge Agent Standalone is selected
  3. Enter the following in the fields:
    1. Name: Pi-Agent
    2. Portainer API server URL: localserver domain [Auto-Fills]
  4. Once all entered, press Create
  5. This will populate new fields, as well as our Join token, that we will need to use to connect the Agent.
  6. Enter EDGE=1 in the Environment Variables field and copy the generated command:
docker run -d \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v /var/lib/docker/volumes:/var/lib/docker/volumes \
  -v /:/host \
  -v portainer_agent_data:/data \
  --restart always \
  -e EDGE=1 \
  -e EDGE_ID=58634afe-3c32-4113-8322-6ed18ef29c60 \
  -e EDGE_KEY=aHR0cHM6Ly8xOTIuMTY4LjUwLjE3MTo5NDQzfDE5Mi4xNjguNTAuMTcxOjgwMDB8ekJlVGt3dW1qaVBHb2FnUVY0WFUwd1ZCU2M1UjEzNUw5T0tZTWphSmUwTT18Ng \
  -e EDGE_INSECURE_POLL=1 \
  -e EDGE=1 \
  --name portainer_edge_agent \
  portainer/agent:2.39.5

docs.title: Setup via Pi Device
docs.text:
SSH onto the Raspberry Pi, and paste the command in to run. The Edge Key will already contain the generated key on Portainer, so no amendments are needed.

Confirm the command has ran, and the docker container for the agent has installed successfully via docker ps. This should show a new container on the Pi named portainer/agent.

Once the docker container is running, go back onto the Portainer Portal, and click on the Home tab. We can then confirm whether this is showing as running, and pulling our containers correctly:

![[Pasted image 20260811192707.png]]

Pi-Agent > Containers

![[Pasted image 20260811192743.png]]

As we can see above, the Raspberry Pi Docker Containers now show under the Pi-Agent environment, seeing our PiHole, Unbound, VaultWarden, MKDocs and the Agent itself.

docs.title: 1. RClone Setup
docs.text:
With the current setup (pre-NAS Server), I have been using RClone, which can be used to backup chosen folders of data from the Raspberry Pi, and upload to a Cloud Service. For my chosen Cloud Service, I have decided to use Proton Drive.

Note: This was done as the root user, using command sudo su

To start, we can first install RClone via the following command:

sudo -v ; curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash

Once installed, we will need to proceed on setting up the config. This will trigger prompts for setting up our backups to the Cloud Service:

rclone config

Proceed with the following options:

  1. Enter n to start a new remote.
  2. This will prompt for a name. I have entered 'ProtonDrive'.
  3. We will then need to pick our Cloud Service. Choose 43 for Proton Drive.
  4. For this service, enter the email address used for the Cloud Service Login.
  5. Choose the option for entering your password to the Cloud Service Account.
  6. Enter the 2FA code tied to your Cloud Service Account (6-digit Code).
  7. Do not enter a secret key, or editing the advanced config when prompted.

Once the setup is complete, run the command below to check that RClone is picking up the Cloud Service folders present on the account:

rclone lsd ProtonDrive:

For example, in my Proton Drive, I have folder 'Raspberry Pi Backups' present, which this command outputs.

We can now proceed on creating the backup script. I have navigated to /etc/backups, where this script will sit. The following is set inside of file backupscr.sh:

#!/bin/bash

# ==== Configuration ====
REMOTE_NAME="ProtonDrive"
DESTINATION_BASE="Raspberry Pi Backups"
SOURCES=( "/home/user" "/etc/" ) #The two folders we want to back up
TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S")
DESTINATION="$REMOTE_NAME:$DESTINATION_BASE/$TIMESTAMP"
FILELIST="/tmp/rclone_files.txt"
# =======================

# Clear previous file list
> "$FILELIST"

echo "Starting backup to: $DESTINATION"

# Collect all files from each source folder
for SRC in "${SOURCES[@]}"; do
    if [ -d "$SRC" ]; then
        find "$SRC" -type f >> "$FILELIST"
        echo "Added files from: $SRC"
    else
        echo "Warning: $SRC is not a valid folder. Skipping."
    fi
done

# Run rclone to copy the files while preserving full paths
rclone copy / "$DESTINATION" \
    --files-from "$FILELIST" \
    --create-empty-src-dirs \
    --copy-links \
    --progress

echo "Backup finished!"

This backs up both the /etc/ folder, and the /home/user/ folder. To make this script executable, run the following:

sudo chmod +x backupscr.sh

You can then run this manually via the following command:

./your_script_name.sh

docs.title: 1. Router DDNS & Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Before we get started, we need to setup our router for port forwarding on port 51820, and enabling DDNS.

  • A Dynamic DNS service is used to automatically update the IP Address if and when it changes. This is useful to use for our VPN, as if the Router reboots, we won't need to manually update the public IP again for our VPN to use.
  • Port forwarding allow us to open port 51820, so that we can connect through to the local network via this.

These steps will go through the ASUS Router settings.

docs.title: Port Forward
docs.text:
Log into your router dashboard, usually being 192.168.x.1.

On the dashboard, under Advanced Settings, click WAN > Virtual Server / Port Forwarding.

The page will show a table of where your port forwarded ports will show. Press Add Profile, and fill in the following information:

![[Pasted image 20260820180307.png]]

Service Name - Name of your choosing Protocol - BOTH External Port - 51820 Internal IP Address - localserver IP of where your PiVPN service will be hosted on Press OK to confirm settings.

docs.title: DDNS Service
docs.text:
On the same router dashboard, navigate to WAN > DDNS. On this page, we can fill in the following details:

  • DDNS - Toggle ON
  • Server - WWW.ASUS.COM
  • Host name - Name of your choosing (.asuscomm.com)
  • HTTPS/SSL Certificate - Auto

Then press Apply.

We can check if this has applied and registered successfully, checking under Network Map > Internet Status > DDNS name

![[Pasted image 20260820190425.png]]

docs.title: 2. Admin Portal
docs.text:
The admin portal for Vaultwarden can be access via domain vault.fooney.xyz/admin. When loading the webpage, it will request for the Authentication key:

![[Pasted image 20260818215308.png]]

This is related to the Argon2 PHC string generated, which is shown in [[1. Installation & Setup]]. For the authentication key, enter the admin password setup when running the temporary docker container.

docs.title: General Setting Checks
docs.text:
Under the Settings tab, we can check if new sign-ups are enabled under the General settings:

![[Pasted image 20260818220146.png]]

By default, this is set to false. This makes it so only one account is active, and any further account creations are disabled. We can test this on the login page by clicking Create Account, and entering a test email. We should receive the following error:

![[Pasted image 20260818220251.png]]

docs.title: Users Tab
docs.text:
The users tab will show us the currently active accounts, and the ability to remove, disable, or invite new users to the system.

Regardless of the Allow new signups setting, we can add additional users via the Invite User section, by adding their email address:

![[Pasted image 20260818220444.png]]

docs.title: Diagnostics Tab
docs.text:
The diagnostics tab will display the following:

![[Pasted image 20260818230212.png]]

Things to note: 1. The Server Installed field will display if and when the image is out of date, and needs updating 2. If Internet Access has an error, and cannot reach the Github page, then the DNS is not set correctly under the compose file 3. If the Websocket field has error'd, this will mean the Nginx proxy server block is configured incorrectly

These as of current, are running as expected with no errors.

docs.title: 2. Configuration Files & HTTP
docs.text:
To start setting up our reverse proxy, we will need to create a new configuration file, that will host our setup. This is found under /etc/nginx/sites-available.

Instead of editing the default config file, we instead want to create a new server block file where we can add on our related proxy settings.

docs.title: Configuring the server blocks
docs.text:
First, create a new file, preferably named the domain (e.g. user.local) in /etc/nginx/sites-available

cd /etc/nginx/sites-available
sudo touch your.sites

We can then edit the file:

sudo nano your.sites

And paste the following template, and replace parameters accoringly:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.com www.example.com http://www.example.com; #Replace with your domain/IP           
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://localhost:3000; #Backend server URL/port           
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;           
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For 
        $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;           
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;       
    }   
}

Press CTRL + S to save the file.

docs.title: Activating the server block
docs.text:
To activate the server block, we want to create a symlink from sites-available, where the server block file sits, to sites-enabled. This is because sites-available isnt our active files for the proxy, but anything in sites-enabled is.

sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/example.com /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/

docs.title: Disabling the landing page
docs.text:
Once created, we can also go ahead and disable the default nginx landing page, if not needed (optional).

sudo unlink /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default

docs.title: Testing it's configuration
docs.text:
We can then test the nginx configuration for any syntax errors:

sudo nginx -t

If all good, we can then reload nginx to apply the changes:

sudo systemctl reload nginx

docs.title: 2. Installation for PiVPN
docs.text:
Pivpn is a easy-to-use script we can run, that will allow us to install our chosen VPN Protocols. In this case, we will be installing Wireguard via this script. This Wireguard VPN will allow us to access the services hosted on our Pi, as well as the Proxmox server, from outside of the local network. This will connect us to the network, as if we're a device within the network.

PLEASE NOTE: This guide assumes you have already setup Pihole + Unbound. If not, please refer to [1. Installation].

docs.title: Installation Command
docs.text:
To get started, we can simply run the installation command here:

curl -L https://install.pivpn.io | bash
  • If sudo apt update has not been ran beforehand, this will automatically run, and update any packages available.

docs.title: GUI Steps
docs.text:
This will initiate a GUI Installation. Follow through the prompts as below:

  1. Press OK

  2. Press OK - We already have static IP address 192.164.x.x set.

  3. Select Yes, as this is still a good idea so that it stops private data from leaking if it uses ipv6 in the future.

  4. Press space on eth0, which is the Ethernet connection used for the Pi. If using Wi-Fi, select WAN, and press OK.

  5. Press Yes, as DCHP Reservation is being used for IP 192.168.x.x.

  6. Press OK, and select user or the main local account you're using for the Pi.

  7. Select Wireguard using the spacebar, and press OK.

  8. Stick with port 51820, and press Ok (We will ensure this is port forwarded on the Router config later on) then Confirm.

  9. Select PiVPN-is-local-DNS by using the spacebar, and pressing OK. As noted, as we're using unbound, we should select this option.

  10. Choose DNS Entry.

  11. Enter the domain name that we set earlier under [1. Router DDNS & Port Forwarding]. This will be x.asuscomm.com.

  12. We will then have confirmation that the server keys will be generated. Press OK.

  13. This will recommend enabling unattended-upgrades. We can confirm, and press Yes, as this is an important feature to enable for automatic security package updates.

  14. This will then confirm the installation has complete. Press OK, and press Yes to confirm reboot.

We can then move on to creating our client.

    ![[Pasted image 20260819215530.png]]

  14. This will then confirm the installation has complete. Press OK, and press Yes to confirm reboot.

We can then move on to creating our client.

docs.title: 2. Project Repository Setup
docs.text: Next, we want to create our repository on Github. These steps were used to create my public repository Pi-Homelab as part of my Raspberry Pi Project, as user f0oney.

docs.title: GitHub Repository Creation
docs.text:
Firstly, we want to create a new repository via Github. Login to the Github main homepage, and click New. This opens the new Github repository page. Fill in the details, and set this to private for the time being.

Repository for the Raspberry Pi Homelab is named Pi-Homelab, and linked here: https://github.com/f0oney/Pi-Homelab

Once created, we can then move over to the Raspberry Pi, to create our project repo folder, where we will link this across to the created GitHub Repo.

docs.title: Repo folder structure on Server/Device
docs.text:
On your device, under /home/user/, we can create a new folder named after your project. For this example, we can user PiProject, via the following command:

sudo mkdir PiProject
cd /home/home/PiProject

Inside of this folder, we can then run the git command below, to create the repo files:

sudo git init -b main

Once the git files have been created, we can start structuring this repo folder, by adding in the separate folders for each of your services. For me, I have vaultwarden and pihole-unbound that I can add in as sub-folders:

sudo mkdir -p /home/user/PiProject/vaultwarden
sudo mkdir -p /home/user/PiProject/pihole-unbound

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
We can then create a .gitignore file, which allows us to specify files we do not want to have show up under our GitHub repository. These can include .env files, or .db files to name a couple.

sudo nano .gitignore

I have then entered the following file types (* meaning any word used):

.env *.env *.db *.sqlite *.sqlite-journal

docs.title: Remote Origin
docs.text:
Next step is to add the remote origin, that links to our private repository created in GitHub, via the following:

sudo git remote add origin https://github.com/user/PiProject

docs.title: Stage and Commits
docs.text:
Once satisfied, we then want to stage the current structure and updates done to this project folder:

git add .

This can then be followed by commiting the changes, so that it saves it locally:

sudo git commit -m "Initial homelab setup and folder structure"
  • The comment in the speech marks adds a comment on the github page, once the changes have been made.

docs.title: Push
docs.text:
We can then finally push these files and changes to the GitHub repository, by using the push command:

sudo git push -u origin main
  • This pushes it to the main branch of the repository.
  • Command will prompt for github username, but also the github password.
  • The Github password will require you to create a Personal Token Key within the Developer settings of GitHub. Recommend generating a classic token key, and then copying this into the console.

Tip: We can add --force, if there is already a README folder in, that we are happy with replacing when the pull command is initiated.

docs.title: 2. Schedule using Crontab
docs.text:
I've set crontab to run every Saturday, at 3AM, using the backup script located in /home/fooney/raspberrypi-homelab/. Done this by:

Crontab - e

Press option 1

In the file, we've added the following line:

0 3 * * 6 /home/user/homelab/backupscr.sh

These parameters state it will run every week, on a Saturday. We can use the following website that will help show which parameters we will need to use:

https://crontab.guru/#0_3___6

The following explains each part of the syntax:

  • 1: Minute (between 0 and 59)
  • 2: Hour (between 0 and 23)
  • 3: Day (between 1 and 31)
  • 4: Month (between 1 and 12)
  • 5: Day of week (between 0 and 7, starting on Sunday)

docs.title: 2. Unbound Config Files
docs.text:
Once the containers are installed, we can then proceed on creating the Unbound files. These aren't necessary, due to the container already pre-generating these in the background, but we can create these manually under /home/user/PiProject-homelab-data/unbound if we want to edit and create custom configs.

These will then mirror over to /etc/unbound/custom.conf.d, as directed on the directory setting of Unbound on the .yaml file - [Raspberry Pi/Pihole & Unbound/1. Installation|1. Installation].

Then, any files mirror'd to custom.conf.d, Unbound will pick up, and use over it's default configs.

Firstly, lets ensure the /etc/unbound/custom.conf.d folder is created. If not already, cd to /etc/, and enter the following commands:

cd /etc/
mkdir unbound
cd unbound/
mkdir custom.conf.d

We will then need to cd over to /home/user/ProjectPi-homelab-data/unbound, and can create the following files:

docs.title: unbound.conf
docs.text:
sudo nano unbound.conf

server:
    verbosity: 1
    interface: 0.0.0.0 # Listening on all network interfaces, so it can accept traffic coming in from the Docker bridge network 172.x.x.x
    port: 53
    do-ip4: yes
    do-udp: yes
    do-tcp: yes

    # May be set to yes if you have IPv6 connectivity
    do-ip6: yes

    # Use this only when you downloaded the list of primary root servers!
    root-hints: /etc/unbound/custom.conf.d/root.hints

    # Trust glue only if it is within the servers authority
    harden-glue: yes

    # Require DNSSEC data for trust-anchored zones, if no DNSSEC data for an answer,
    # with trust anchors enabled, the zone becomes Bogus
    harden-dnssec-stripped: yes

    # Don't use capitalization randomization
    use-caps-for-id: no

    # Reduce EDNS reassembly buffer size
    edns-buffer-size: 1472

    # Perform prefetching of close to expired message cache entries
    prefetch: yes

    # Min and Max time DNS Records are cached for, in seconds
    cache-min-ttl: 3600
    cache-max-ttl: 86400

    # One thread should be sufficient
    num-threads: 1

    # Ensure kernel buffer is large enough (reduced to avoid permission warnings)
    so-rcvbuf: 400k

    # Respond to queries from local networks only
    access-control: 127.0.0.0/8 allow
    access-control: 10.0.0.0/8 allow
    access-control: 172.16.0.0/12 allow
    access-control: 192.168.0.0/16 allow

    # Ensure privacy of local IP ranges
    private-address: 192.168.0.0/16
    private-address: 169.254.0.0/16
    private-address: 172.16.0.0/12
    private-address: 10.0.0.0/8
    private-address: fd00::/8
    private-address: fe80::/10

docs.title: root.hints
docs.text:
sudo touch root.hints

sudo curl -o /etc/unbound/root.hints https://www.internic.net/domain/named.root

This should output the following:

;       This file holds the information on root name servers needed to
;       initialize cache of Internet domain name servers
;       (e.g. reference this file in the "cache  .  <file>"
;       configuration file of BIND domain name servers).
;

;       under anonymous FTP as
;           file                /domain/named.cache
;           on server           FTP.INTERNIC.NET
;       -OR-                    RS.INTERNIC.NET
;

;       related version of root zone:     2026072901
;
; FORMERLY NS.INTERNIC.NET
;

A.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.      3600000      A     198.41.0.4
A.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.      3600000      AAAA  2001:503:ba3e::2:30

B.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.      3600000      A     170.247.170.2

It is recommended to update the root.hints file once every 6 months, as domains may update by InterNic. We can simply use the second command above to re-generate the file and it's contents.

docs.title: dnsmaq.d
docs.text:
We can also configure and create our custom configuration file for dnsmasq. This is located in /home/user/ProjectPi-homelab-data/dnsmaq.d, which we can cd into, and run command sudo nano 02-lan-access.conf, entering the following config:

# Allow all interfaces
listen-address=0.0.0.0
bind-interfaces
domain-needed
bogus-priv
EOF

docs.title: resolv.conf
docs.text:
To prevent DNS leaks, we can set resolv.conf to use Pihole, and also ensure it is immutable so that we prevent the DHCP from changing it:

echo "nameserver 127.0.0.1" | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf
sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf

docs.title: dhclient
docs.text:
We can set in the dhclient.conffile to point to domain server 127.0.0.1:

sudo nano /etc/dhcp/dhclient.conf

#Add in the file
supersede domain-name-servers 127.0.0.1;

docs.title: Docker DNS
docs.text:
We will also need to configure the Docker DNS via the daemon.json file. To do this, create or edit /etc/docker/daemon.json

sudo nano /etc/docker/daemon.json

#Add in the file
{
    "dns": ["127.0.0.1"]
}

docs.title: 3. Create a Client
docs.text: A client is essentially a individual tunnel that you can use to connect your device to the local network. It is heavily recommended to create separate clients for each device. This example will walk through creating one for my laptop.

docs.title: Client Process
docs.text:
To start creating one, simply run the command below:

pivpn -a

This will prompt to enter the Client IP from range. You can either enter one yourself, or press enter to let Pivpn pick one for you:

::: Chosen Client IP: random IP

It will then ask for the name of the client. You will receive confirmation that this has been created successfully.

docs.title: Adding Tunnel to the Wireguard Mobile App
docs.text:
We can use command pivpn -qr, and enter the client name, to generate the QR of the client. This can be scanned from the Wireguard Phone App.

To do this, open the Wireguard app and press the + symbol, selecting Scan from QR code. This should then add the tunnel to your app for use.

docs.title: Adding Tunnel to the Wireguard Desktop App
docs.text:
To add the tunnel to your Desktop app, we will need to physically save the .conf file of the client, and add to the application. These client .conf files are located in /home/user/configs.

To download this file onto our laptop, I am using application MobaXTerm, which will let me physically right-click the file within the file directory pane, and press Download:

![[Pasted image 20260819222725.png]]

Once downloaded, we can open Wireguard and navigate through the following:

  1. Click Add Tunnel
  2. Locate the saved .conf file, and double-click to open
  3. You should then see the tunnel appear on your list. Press Activate to start up the VPN.

docs.title: 3. OpenSSL Self Signed Certificates
docs.text:
OpenSSL is the service we will use to create our certificates, which will allow us to use HTTPS against our local domains. OpenSSL is recommended for self-signed certificates, as noted by Lets Encrypt via their Documentation.

'Self-Signed' certificates are certificates signed by the creator's own private key, rather then a trusted third-party Certificate Authority. This allows us to complete this completely offline, whilst having the basic encryption needed for our web portals.

The downside to this setup however, is that we would need to manually download the certificate onto each device, and add to the web browser being used. This means that the certificates are not trusted by anyone else, but for local development, this is fine.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To get started, we can install OpenSSL via the following command:

sudo apt install openssl

docs.title: Folder Structures
docs.text:
Once installed, we next need to create a folder where we will store the certificates. In this case, I will be creating a folder named openssl under /etc/openssl:

cd /etc/
mkdir openssl
cd /etc/openssl

In the folder, we can begin running our commands to create the certificates.

docs.title: Creating the Certificates
docs.text:
Firstly, we will need to create the key for the CA Certificate. This will be named userCA.key. The following command is ran below:

openssl genrsa -des3 -out userCA.key 4096

Then, we will need to generate the CA certificate itself with the created CA key, named userCA.crt. This will prompt for the information required for the certificate…

openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -key userCA.key -out userCA.crt

The info it requests will be as follows:

  • Country Name (2 letter code)
  • State or Province Name
  • City
  • Organisation Name
  • Organisational Unit Name
  • Common Name (e.g. server FQDN or YOUR name)
  • Email Address

The information does not need to be real, and you can enter fake information, such as a fake name. This is because no public authority checks these.

Once the CA root certificate is created, we can then proceed with creating the wildcard custom domain certificate. This allows us to use the certificate for any local domains using *.user.local, named user.key:

openssl genrsa -out user.key 2048

We will now need to create the config file openssl.cnf, which we are going to use for CSR and signing. The CSR is a Certificate Signing Request, which is a message sent to the CA (Certificate Authority) to apply for a certificate. To create and start the config file, we can run:

Sudo nano openssl.conf

Then, the following can be entered in the config file itself:

[req]
default_md = sha256
prompt = no
req_extensions = req_ext
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name

[req_distinguished_name]
commonName = *.user.xyz
countryName = YOUR_COUNTRY
stateOrProvinceName = No state
localityName = No City
organizationName = No Company

[req_ext]
keyUsage=critical,digitalSignature,keyEncipherment
extendedKeyUsage=critical,serverAuth,clientAuth
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[alt_names]
DNS.1=user.local
DNS.2=*.user.local

We can then use this to create the CSR:

openssl req -new -nodes -key user.key -config openssl.cnf -out user.csr

We can finally then sign this with the created CA. The final certificate that we can use will be named user.crt:

openssl x509 -req -in user.csr -CA userCA.crt -CAkey userCA.key -CAcreateserial -out user.crt -days 1024 -sha256 -extfile openssl.cnf -extensions req_ext

With the certificates and keys created, we can organise these into sub folders within the OpenSSL folder:

/etc/openssl/ca_certificates userCA.crt /etc/openssl/ca_keys userCA.key /etc/openssl/certificates user.crt /etc/openssl/keys user.key

docs.title: Installing the Certificates
docs.text:
For us to be able to use these on our devices, we will need to install them on each individual device. As I am using MobaXTerm for accessing the Pi console via SSH, I can simply navigate to the file directory via the file directory tree (found on the left side of the application).

We want to install the userCA.crt certificate on the device, via /etc/openssl/ca_certificates, by highlighting the file > right-click > press Download.

Once this is on our machine, we can then share this on other devices by any preferable method. The steps on installing the certificate is slightly different however.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: We can simply follow the steps found under #Trusted-Root-CA, on [[Router HTTPS Configuration]]. This will guide you on how to add the certificate to the Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
Under the settings, navigate through the following settings:

  1. Click on Security and privacy > More security settings > Install from device storage > CA certificate
  2. Choose Install anyway
  3. Enter your device password or biometrics
  4. Find the file in your storage, and click Done

docs.title: Browser
docs.text:
We can also add it to our browsers, via it's certificate settings. Steps vary depending on browser, but for Firefox, this can be done via:

  1. Click on Privacy and Security
  2. Choose Advanced settings under Connection and software security
  3. Scroll down to Certificates, and choose Manage Certificates
  4. Press Import, and select the certificate stored on your device

docs.title: 3. Router DNS Configuration
docs.text: With Pihole + Unbound now setup, we lastly need to make sure that all devices connected to the local network, is using this configuration as it's DNS. Currently, all devices will still use the default router's DNS settings, so therefore, Pihole with Unbound is completely bypassed. To change this, we will need to go onto the router's portal and amend it.

docs.title: Router Steps
docs.text:
For my setup, I have obtained a third party router, specifically model RT-AX52 Pro by ASUS. I had to purchase one of these, to allow me to add custom configurations for DNS, as well as other features and settings I would not get with my default router provided by my ISP, due to custom configurations being locked down.

  1. Firstly, login to your router via it's local IP on the browser, usually 192.168.0.1. For ASUS, it will prompt for my username and password which I set in it's setup.
  2. Once logged in, navigate to LAN under Advanced Settings, and then click on the DHCP Server Tab.
  3. Look for fields DNS Server 1 and DNS Server 2, under DNS and WINS Server Setting.
  4. On both these fields, enter the Raspberry Pi's IP Address, where Pihole and Unbound is hosted on. Again, this will usually be something like 192.168.0.x.

![[Pasted image 20260817213054.png]]

  • We want both servers set to this, so that it does not have any chance in using another DNS Server.

  • Press Apply. This will reboot the router, and apply the changes.

The networks DNS should now use the Raspberry Pi's IP, which both Pihole and Unbound are hosted on, and direct all queries to this going forward. Any device on the network will therefore use this going forward.

docs.title: 3. Shared Repository Files
docs.text: Inside of /home/user/PiProject (your named repo folder), we want to add in the files we would like to share to our GitHub repository. We need to be careful with how we do this however, as we do not want to share sensitive information such as API keys.

docs.title: Seperating shared data and non-shared data with Github
docs.text:
For my setup, I have therefore created an additional folder for what files I would like to keep off Github, using ProjectPi as the example:

/home/user/PiProject/ - Contains /pihole-unbound, only hosting the unbound files and the compose.yaml

/home/user/PiProject-Data/ - Contains data relating to the services, that I do not want hosted on GitHub. This includes the main pihole configuration files, dnsmasq.d, and other sensitive service data

The Pihole configuration folder is an example of one that we do not want to share on Github, as this contains site history, queries, client activity, and Gravity.

docs.title: 4. HTTPS Configuration
docs.text: With the self-signed certificates created, we can use these to create our HTTPS connections to the local domains. For this example, we will use our Pihole server block we setup previously under [2. Configuration Files & HTTP], to add on HTTPS capability.

docs.title: Server Block Amendments
docs.text:
Navigate to the server block created earlier via sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/your.sites, and add the additional lines:

server {
    listen 443 ssl; # https port
    listen [::]:80; # used for ipv6
    server_name example.com  www.example.com;

    ssl_certificate /etc/openssl/certificates/user.crt; # Locations of the certs
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/openssl/keys/user.key; # Location of the keys

   location / {

       proxy_pass http://localhost:${PORT};  # Backend server URL/port
       proxy_set_header Host $host;
       proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
   }
}
  • ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key lines are added, so that the certificate crt and key are obtained and used in it's connection.
  • listen 443 ssl is used in replacement of port 80, as this is the https port.
  • listen [::]:80 is used for ipv6 connections.

docs.title: HTTPS Redirect
docs.text:
To redirect http requests to https, we can add the following server block on top:

server {
    listen 80; # http port
    listen [::]:80; # used for ipv6

    server_name example.com www.example.com;
    return 301 https://example.com/admin;
}

docs.title: Checking for syntax errors
docs.text:
With the Pihole server block now complete, we can check for syntax errors, before applying the changes:

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

For other server blocks setup for the Raspberry Pi services, please direct to the Server Blocks Breakdown section.

docs.title: 4. Pihole Web Interface Login & Checks
docs.text: Next, is logging into the Pihole Interface, and a quick overview of what we can do, and the settings available to us.

docs.title: IP & Local Domain
docs.text:
To first load up the Pihole Interface, we will need to enter your IP Address in the Address Bar. Example being: http://192.168.x.x:${PORT}

With Nginx, we can set this up against a local domain, something like https://pihole.user.local, with HTTPS enabled with self-signed certs. You can find how these were setup via [Insert guide links], but for the time being, after initial setup without Nginx and Self-Signed Certs, the IP Address mentioned above will allow you onto the login page with HTTP.

docs.title: Main Portal Page
docs.text:
Once loaded, we will be presented with the login page. Enter the password setup from the installation guide [1. Installation], which was set on the compose file.

![[Pasted image 20260815162538.png|394]]

Once logged in, we will be presented with the main dashboard. This will show the current status, total queries made, queries blocked, and client activity. We can also view the Upstream Servers widget, which shows which servers are actioning the queries.

We can specifically click on certain widgets on the dashboard, such as Total Queries, which will take us to the report, and also provide live feeds of what's coming in.

docs.title: Unbound Checks
docs.text:
On the Dashboard, find the Upstream Servers widget, and check over which upstream servers are appearing:

![[Pasted image 20260815162849.png|397]]

We can see for example, that our Unbound DNS is working, as it is showing with private IP Address 172.21.0.2#53, which is used by the Unbound Docker container (Docker containers usually use 172.x.x.x). Inside the docker container itself, it will be using IP 127.0.0.1.

These next settings should be set automatically by the installation, but good to check anyway. Under Settings > DNS, untick all Upstream DNS Servers, and add on the Unbound custom DNS as so:

In the same area, also set Interface settings to 'Permit all origins'. **Note: As mentioned, this may be set already by the Compose file. If so, this will be greyed out, and you cannot change it. This would only be changeable by amending the Compose file, and re-creating the Docker container.

This setting needs to be set to 'Permit all origins', as this allows both our Pihole and Unbound docker containers to communicate with each other. This is due to them both using separate docker networks, showing as this they're coming from outside the local subnet.

We can lastly run two commands in the console, to check that it is returning our container's 172.x.x.x IP as the DNS Domain:

# Check if Pihole is using Unbound
docker exec -it pihole2026050 nslookup example.com unbound

# Test from another device
nslookup example.com 192.168.50.44

Both should return the following:

unbound

Server: unbound
Address: 172.21.0.3#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name: example.com
Address 104.20.32.154

192.168.x.x

Server: 192.168.x.x
Address: 192.168.x.x#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name: example.com
Address: 172.66.147.243

The unbound block will show 172.x.x.x if successful, showing that it is using the docker IP for the unbound container.

The 192.168.x.x will show the same IP if successful, showing that your external device is successfully reaching Pihole.

docs.title: 5. DNS Settings
docs.text:
For domains using Nginx, to redirect to specified IPs + Ports, we need to add each local domain entry to point to the Raspberry Pi IP, where Nginx is hosted.

This is so that once the request is received to connect onto the local domain, it is forwarded straight to Nginx, that then deals with the reverse proxy side.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For example, Proxmox is currently hosted on a different server using IP example 192.168.0.56, and port 8005. The reverse proxy is setup on Nginx, hosted on 192.168.0.44, with code blocks setup in file /etc/nginx/sites-available/your.sites (refer to the Proxmox note under Nginx RP Blocks folder). The IP that proxmox.user.local points to will therefore be 192.168.0.44, as we want to forward it to Nginx to deal with:

![[Pasted image 20260730224916.png]]

docs.title: Simple Local Domain Setup via Pihole
docs.text:
Other domains that do not need to be managed by Nginx, can point directly to their designated IPs. To find the configuration for this, and add new domains, we can follow through these simple steps:

  1. In the Pihole admin portal, navigate to Settings > Local DNS Records
  2. In the Local DNS records pane, within the Domain table, enter the full domain name, alongside it's associated IP
  3. Once entered, click the green + symbol

docs.title: 6. Domain Block Lists
docs.text:
One of the main features of Pihole, is it's ability to block numerous queries and domains on a network level, meaning any device connected to the network it's running on, will have these domains automatically blocked. This is particularly useful for blocking ADs!

With Pihole up and running, we can add a block list via the Web Interface, which is essentially a simple list full of domains we want to block.

docs.title: Obtaining a blocklist URL link
docs.text:
To find a particular block list to add to our Pihole, we can search the web for various lists created by the community. For me, I have used Hagezi's Ultimate blocklist, found on his GitHub page. You can find this on the following URL: https://github.com/hagezi/dns-blocklists

To obtain the blocklist link, scroll down the README, and save the 'Adblock' link (which states it can be used for Pihole) under the intensity level you'd like to choose:

![[Pasted image 20260817214434.png]]

This method will be similar on any other GitHub page, or site you use, by copying the link to the list.

PLEASE NOTE - The blocklist I am currently using, is considered aggressive, and therefore may break certain websites. I therefore tend to manually permit certain domains if I find them to completely break sites that I want to visit, which I will show how to do further down this section.

docs.title: Adding to Pihole
docs.text:
Once you've obtained the link to the blocklist you'd like to add, we can follow the steps below to add this to Pihole:

  1. Login to Pihole, using the login details setup in the installation process.
  2. Navigate to Lists under Group Management
  3. Here, you will see the Add a new subscribed list panel, and the Subscribed lists panel. Currently, your subscribed lists should be empty. This will be where your active lists will sit. To add a new list, we will need to paste the saved blocklist URL we obtained earlier into the Address field, and add a chosen comment: ![[Pasted image 20260817214929.png]]
  4. Press Add blocklist
  5. This will then appear under your Subscribed lists, with status Enabled:

![[Pasted image 20260817215039.png]]

docs.title: Allowing certain domains
docs.text:
As mentioned previously, if you have an aggressive blocklist, that may have broken a particular website you're using, it is handy to be able to allow that particular domain through as an exception. To do this, we first will need to identify which domain is being blocked. We can find this by using the Query Log.

Load or perform the certain action that is not working correctly, e.g. Facebook comments, and look for the domain that is being blocked during that moment. For example, as soon as I attempt to open Facebook comments, I can find the following being blocked:

![[Pasted image 20260817221504.png]]

A quick way to allow these through, is to click on Allow as highlighted in the screenshot above. Once allowed, we can view these in the Domains tab, under Group Management:

![[Pasted image 20260817221613.png]]

On these entries, you can add a comment to note the reason for allowing it, so you can easily keep track. I would then recommend updating the Gravity list, to apply the changes...

docs.title: Updating Gravity List
docs.text:
When you have added a new blocklist, it is always recommended to immediately update the gravity list via Pihole. The gravity list is the main compiled database of blocked domains, where Pihole downloads the addresses from your subscribed lists, combines them, and removes any duplicates that may crop up when you have multiple lists. Once updated, all your lists should be active on Pihole.

To do this, click through the following settings:

  1. In the Pihole interface, click on Tools > Update Gravity
  2. Click Update
  3. You should see the following command portal appear, showing you if the update was successful. Any errors will also appear if it has failed to update all: ![[Pasted image 20260817215712.png]]

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Throughout the guides, many directories, IPs, and usernames will be defaulted to the below list. This is to benefit my privacy. The below are as follows:

  • /home/user
    • User being your set username
  • ${PORT}
    • Your chosen port
  • x.user.local
    • Your local domain, x being the service
  • localserver
    • Your server IP

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Welcome to my Documentation Hub. This is where all my documentation regarding my current Raspberry Pi and Proxmox server Projects are hosted.

This allows me to share the work I have done, and all the steps and configuration. This is hosted via GitHub Pages, with the site pages created using MKDocs (with Material).

Any configuration files that are shareable, will be held on my GitHub repo, named Pi-Homelab. You can get to this using the link found at the top-right corner of the site.

To get started, click on any of the left-side tabs.

docs.title: Portainer Server Block
docs.text:
This is a similar structure to Proxmox:

server {
    listen 80; # http port
    listen [::]:80; # used for ipv6

    server_name portainer.user.local www.portainer.user.local;
    return 301 https://portainer.user.local;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    server_name portainer.user.local www.portainer.user.local;

    ssl_certificate /etc/openssl/certificates/user.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/openssl/keys/user.key;

   location / {

       proxy_pass https://localserver:${PORT};
       proxy_http_version 1.1;
       proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
       proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";

       proxy_set_header Host $host;
       proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

       proxy_buffering off;
       client_max_body_size 0;
   }
}

docs.title: Proxmox Server Block
docs.text:
Proxmox had to be setup slightly differently for this code block.

As Proxmox relies on SSL, HTTPS connection, we needed to make sure that 'https' is used in the 'proxy_pass' line, and that additional proxy headers are used. See the full code block below:

server {
    listen 80; # http port
    listen [::]:80; # used for ipv6

    server_name proxmox.user.local www.proxmox.user.local;
    return 301 https://proxmox.user.local;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    server_name proxmox.user.local www.proxmox.user.local;

    ssl_certificate /etc/openssl/certificates/user.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/openssl/keys/user.key;

   location / {

       # Ensuring 'https' is used in the below line, instead of 'http'
       proxy_pass https://localserver:${PORT};
       proxy_http_version 1.1;
       proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
       proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";

       # The additional headers used
       proxy_set_header Host $host;
       proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

       proxy_buffering off;
       client_max_body_size 0;
   }
}

The comments in the code blocks above show what has been amended, and what has been added.

docs.title: Router HTTPS Configuration
docs.text: The router HTTPS will need to be setup differently, as opposed to using Nginx. For my Router, I will be using ASUS' in-built Local Config. This will provide us with a certificate, and also setting a HTTPS port against it for access.

docs.title: Router Settings
docs.text:
To enable this, navigate to Administration > System, and scroll down to Local Access Config.

Under the Authentication Method, set this to HTTPS. This will bring up additional fields, allowing us to add the HTTPS port, as well as downloading the certificate.

![[Pasted image 20260820192305.png]]

By default, this can be set to 8443.

Install the certificate by clicking on Export Root Certificate. We can then install the certificate and add to our Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

docs.title: Adding to Trusted Root Certification Authorities
docs.text:
1. Double-click the .crt file that was downloaded, and press Install Certificate
  2. Select Current User, under Store Location. Press Next.
  3. Select Place all certificates in the following store, and press Browse. Double-click Trusted Root Certification Authorities, and press OK.
  4. Press Next and Finish.
  5. Confirm installation, by press Yes.

docs.title: Adding Certificate Snap-ons
docs.text:
1. Launch MMC
  2. Choose File > Add/Remove Snap-ins
  3. Choose Certificates, then choose Add
  4. Choose My user account
  5. Choose Add again, but this time select Computer Account
  6. Press OK
  7. Under Certificates - Current User, navigate to Trusted Root Certification Authorities > Certificates
  8. Find the installed certificate, highlight, and press Copy
  9. Then, navigate to Certificates (Local Computer) > Trusted Root Certification Authorities > Certificates
  10. Press Paste

We can confirm that this loads via HTTPS, by entering the router IP and port 8443 (or port you have used).

docs.title: Vaultwarden Server Block
docs.text:
Example server block setup for Vaultwarden:

upstream vaultwarden-default {
  zone vaultwarden-default 64k;
  server localserver:${PORT};
  keepalive 2;
}


map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      "";
}

server {
    listen 80; # http port
    listen [::]:80; # used for ipv6

    server_name vault.user.local www.vault.user.local;
    return 301 https://vault.user.local;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name vault.user.local www.vault.user.local;

    ssl_certificate /etc/openssl/certificates/user.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/openssl/keys/user.key;

   location / {

       proxy_pass http://vaultwarden-default;

       client_max_body_size 525M;

       proxy_http_version 1.1;
       proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
       proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

       proxy_set_header Host $host;
       proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
       proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
   }
}
